findings.title: The abort-on-another-thread test cannot tell whether release() closed the SSLSocket: the mutant without the SSLSocket close survives
findings.description: isClosed() of a JDK SSLSocketImpl returns tlsIsClosed, which the reading thread sets itself once its read fails on the closed plain socket (SocketException -> handleException -> conContext.fatal -> transport.shutdown). In this test the request thread is blocked in exactly such a read, so after res.abort the SSLSocket reads as closed even if ProxyExchange.release never calls SSLSocket.close(). Removing the SSLSocket close from BackendClient.closeConnection makes the other four new tests fail but leaves this one green. The thread-safety half (abort returns in <1 s) is real; the 'closes the SSLSocket' half is vacuous.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the close() call itself rather than isClosed(): e.g. have RecordingSslSockets hand out a thin delegating SSLSocket (or record via a wrapper) that counts close() invocations and the calling thread, and assert that close() ran on the abort thread; or assert on a socket whose reader is not blocked (abort after the reader returned) so the reader's fatal path cannot set the flag. Re-run the mutant to confirm the test turns red.

findings.drop_reason: No resource is left: the plain socket (the only OS resource on the JDK) is closed by BackendClient.secure, and the leftover JDK SSLSocketImpl holds no native state (its finalizer's close fails fast at getSoLinger on the closed transport). On Android both Conscrypt sockets free/close themselves on any startHandshake exception (FD socket: finally shutdownAndFreeSslNative; engine socket: close() in its catch), which is the R2-001 concern. What remains is an inaccurate javadoc sentence for the JDK timeout case; correcting it ('except a handshake timeout on the JDK, whose socket holds nothing beyond the closed plain socket') is optional.
findings.title: A TLS handshake timeout leaves the JDK SSLSocket unclosed, contrary to the TlsConnector javadoc
findings.description: The new finally closes the SSLSocket only when handshaken; on a handshake timeout (CONNECT_TIMEOUT) the JDK does not close it itself. Harmless on the JDK, correct on Android.
findings.suggested_fix: Optional: fix the javadoc claim, or close the SSLSocket after plain for every failure once createSocket returned (safe: with plain closed first the JDK close returns at getSoLinger).

findings.title: Cross-thread SSLSocket close from the onAbort listener is only shown non-blocking on the JDK; on Conscrypt close() waits for the pending read
findings.description: The javadoc's guarantee 'takes no lock it would wait for' is JDK-specific (getSoLinger fails before recordLock; readLock only tryLock). On Android API 21+ the default layered socket is Conscrypt, whose close() blocks in awaitPendingOps until the reading thread leaves SSL_read. JDK stress (25 aborts at varied moments, 3 JDKs) shows no blocking and the slot always freed; the limiter is released in a finally after closeConnection, so a slow close delays but never leaks the slot.
findings.suggested_fix: None required unless an Android run shows a stall; if one does, run the SSLSocket close off the listener thread or after the reader's own exit.

resolved_findings.evidence: Every proxy-side end of an https connection now runs BackendClient.closeConnection(plain, ssl): body close (Proxy.SocketBodyStream.close), release (ProxyExchange.release/attach, incl. the onAbort thread), the close before a 502/503 retry (Proxy.lastAttempt) and a post-handshake refusal (TlsConnector.layer finally). Mutant without the SSLSocket close fails 4 of the 5 new tests (body end, read-timeout release, retry close, rejected host name); the abort path closes it by code reading and stress (25 aborts, unclosed=0 on JDK 17/21/8u504), though its test does not discriminate (R3-001). Handshake failures are left to the provider, which on Android (Conscrypt) frees/closes the socket itself (R3-002, dropped).
